Unveiled alongside new iPhones and AirPods at Apple’s Surprise and Shine press event in early September, the Apple Watch Series 12 is the latest and would hope to be the greatest entry in the company’s long line of smartwatches.
Last year’s excellent Series 11 already dominated the premium smartwatch market with ease. To that device’s list of qualities, the Series 12 adds upgraded health sensors, a new app, compelling AI-powered audio features, a more powerful processor, improved fast-charge capabilities, and some lovely new materials and color finishes. It even manages, against all odds, to keep the same starting price as its predecessor amid a torrent of price increases elsewhere.
With Apple refusing to update the mighty Apple Watch SE, the field seems clear for the Series 12 to slot in as the best Apple Watch, and therefore as the best smartwatch on the market. But life is rarely that simple. I spent two weeks with the Apple Watch Series 12, testing and evaluating its design, features, battery performance, and more, all so we can bring you thorough, expert buying advice. Is this the smartwatch for you? Read on to find out.
(For broader advice, check our guide to the best Apple Watch in 2026.)
Apple Watch Series 12 design
As I’ve pointed out in a separate article, the Apple Watch design didn’t change in any fundamental ways this year. It’s the same shape, the same dimensions, the same buttons. Which isn’t necessarily a bad thing, because Apple’s design is a modern classic: a sleek and slimline chassis which feels unobtrusive on the wrist and is intuitive to use. The fundamentals were built to last.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




There’s one non-visible change, which is that the aluminum models get a screen upgrade from Ion-X glass to Ceramic Shield 2 that Apple says is 60 percent tougher. (The more expensive models remain on Sapphire crystal, an even more scratch-resistant material, but one which is more vulnerable to drop impacts–not that drops should be much of an issue for a smartwatch.) That’s not an easy claim to test, and I can’t say I noticed a difference from the previous generation, but it’s a nice bonus in terms of peace of mind.
And then there are the strictly cosmetic differences. But these are absolutely worth mentioning, partly because the Apple Watch is to some degree a fashion accessory, and partly because they’re so great.
The returning ceramic material, for example, looks fantastic in both Pearly White and Night Blue. You’ll have to pay a premium for that option, which starts at $899/£849, so a better bet may be to stick with the cheapest aluminum case material, but pick the new and stunning Dark Bronze finish. Macworld’s review unit is a very smart black unit, but I’ve experienced serious Bronze envy. If you prefer the titanium case, consider the new Radiant Gold finish, which has a gorgeous shine to it. There are lots of opportunities, in other words, to grab a beautiful finish and simultaneously show off that you’ve got the latest model. Maybe the long-awaited design will finally arrive next year (or maybe it’ll be delayed yet again), but in the meantime these surface-level changes are fun and fresh.

				
					

				
			Dark Bronze (left) and Pearl White ceramic (right) are among the lovely new aesthetic options for this year.
Apple




I will raise one quibble concerning the build quality of this generation: the assembly of my Series 12 review sample doesn’t appear quite as flawless as I’ve come to expect from this product line. When I run a finger across the face and on to the surrounding bezel, I can feel a sharp edge where one material gives way to another. For comparison, I immediately checked my two older Apple Watches and found that the SE 3 had a slight edge, but it was less noticeable than the Series 12, while the Series 11 had almost no detectable edge at all.
I don’t know if this is significant–the result of cost cutting, a change in manufacturing tolerances, or some other systemic factor–or if I just got unlucky and received a slightly defective unit. (If it’s the latter, my colleague Mahmoud Itani also got unlucky. He reports the same issue.) I would also like to stress that this is a very minor quibble that doesn’t particularly bother me: When I say sharp, I mean only that it’s hard and sudden, not that there’s any danger of cutting yourself on it. But it’s very unusual to come across imperfections like this when reviewing an Apple product, and not entirely reassuring as an omen of things to come.

				
					

				
			My Series 12 (left) has a sharp edge above the screen whereas the Series 11 (right) is smooth. The difference is hard to see, but easy to feel.
David Price / Foundry




Apple Watch Series 12 performance
It isn’t normally necessary to delve too deep into the tech specs when reviewing a smartwatch. The Series 12 has 64GB of storage, for example, but that’s unlikely to have much of an effect on your day-to-day experience. Its screen has the same number of pixels as on the previous two generations, and the pixel density hasn’t changed since the Series 4; Apple long ago reached a level of sharpness that was adequate for the job and hasn’t bothered changing it since. And while the RAM allocation is unofficially understood to have doubled from 2GB to 4GB this year, you wouldn’t know it from Apple’s published spec sheet or general performance.
One item on the spec sheet that does seem significant, however, is the new S11 processor. Not because the Apple Watch needed more processing power when handling apps; unless you own something really old, it’s unlikely you’re running into major bottlenecks in this area. But because of the new things it allows the Series 12 to do.
Inevitably, AI is a major part of this equation. While older watches dating back to the Series 9 are retrospectively compatible with Siri AI, the Series 12 is the best equipped to handle its demands. And only the Series 12 gets access to the new suite of AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which I’ll discuss in the next section. These, Apple says, are wholly dependent on the S11 chip and specifically its Secure Enclave.
The S11 chip’s power and sophistication should also help with battery performance, something that could prove vital given the inclusion of continuous heart-rate monitoring and the power demands of this feature. (Battery life too will be discussed later in this review.) And Apple says the accuracy of the health sensors themselves is indebted to the capabilities of the S11.
If you’re looking for a general speed boost, however, my experience suggests this isn’t the watch for you. I can’t remember ever finding my Series 11 or my SE 3 sluggish (both have the S10 chip), so it’s hard to see that there was much room for improvement. But worse, from time to time I got the impression that the Series 12 is slower than those models. It’s difficult to be scientific without a benchmarking app, but here are a few subjective examples that gave me a bad feeling about the Series 12’s speed and responsiveness:
Shazam on the watch (triggered manually) once “thought” for so long that the song ended with no information given.
On one occasion, I walked for a full hour and the watch never recognized I was active or suggested a workout.
I went into Activity to check my steps, and it was still showing an old count from an hour previously. It took 10 to 15 seconds to update this, while I watched impatiently.
On another occasion, the watch didn’t offer me a sleep score until 10.25 am, long after I woke up (and after I’d done a full workout, absurdly).
Most irritatingly, three times on a single day, my Series 12 spontaneously reset without being asked.

				
					

				
			The Series 12 deciding to reset itself three times in one day.
David Price / Foundry




There may be explanations for some or all of these annoyances. For example, perhaps Shazam suffered from a poor internet connection rather than a lack of processing muscle (although my iPhone was doing fine at the time), and perhaps I failed to trigger a suggested workout because I was walking slower than usual. It’s also been reported that the watchOS 27.0.1 update has solved the rebooting issue.
But still, I’ve been using one Apple Watch or another nearly every day for well over a decade now, and I can tell you with confidence that I’ve grown to expect better. Whether it’s down to issues with current iterations of watchOS, or processing resources being diverted to new features, my Series 12 simply gives me the subjective vibe of being a little less responsive, a little less reliable, than other Apple Watches I’ve used in the recent past. Which isn’t what you want, or expect, from a device with a powerful new chip.
Apple Watch Series 12 features
With design largely staying the same and tech specs having little impact on the user experience, the burden of convincing customers to upgrade falls heavily on the feature set. On the positive side, this expands in several promising ways this year. The only problem is that quite a few of the new features aren’t actually ready yet.
Take Audio Intelligence, the suite of features loosely grouped under the themes of AI and sound. There are four of these: Sound Recognition, Music Recognition, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. The latter two, which incidentally are by far the most interesting of the set, aren’t currently available, and Apple hasn’t even named a date for their launch. The support document says only that they “will be available in beta later this year, starting with English.”
The morality of this sort of thing is debatable, to say the least. Unsurprisingly, since they’re so futuristic and feel so useful (even if there are privacy and general AI ickiness concerns to be navigated), Live Rewind and Siri Recap were both prominent in the launch presentation. So on some level Apple was hoping to convince people to buy the new devices on the strength of these features, without being prepared to say when the features will arrive. We’ve been here before, and Apple has the legal bills to show for it; hopefully its experience in that case will ensure relatively prompt delivery in this one.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




But back to the features themselves. Here are my thoughts:
Sound Recognition
As long ago as iOS 14, the iPhone was able to identify certain sounds–doorbells, smoke alarms, crying babies–and then notify you if it heard them. It’s a feature with enormous, even life-saving potential for those who are deaf or hard of hearing. This year the feature comes to the Apple Watch, so it won’t matter if you accidentally leave your phone upstairs.
It’s simple, useful, and appears reliable: in each of my tests there was a brief delay of perhaps three seconds after the sound, and then a notification appeared. 
I tested for doorbell, door knock, cat, dog, running water, breaking glass, car horn, and crying baby. The feature detected all of these with virtually 100 percent accuracy when it heard them. Smoke alarm and fire alarm were initially less reliable when I tested them using YouTube videos, which might seem very bad… until it occurred to me that an extremely high volume was probably part of the algorithm. When I used the testing button on an actual smoke alarm, it got a lot more accurate. After these tests, I’m happy to say that Sound Recognition can reliably detect all the sounds it says it can.
But on the other hand there were false positives, and quite a lot of them. Over the course of testing, the watch has mistakenly identified (non-doorbell) sound effects in various TV shows and YouTube videos as a doorbell, or heard me tapping a spoon on a pan to get off the last of the pasta sauce, for example, and interpreted this as a door knock. It surprisingly frequently thinks there’s a dog nearby (but very rarely a cat, for some reason) and has more than once alarmed me by claiming to hear broken glass when I’m only putting away crockery.
So it’s a clever and quite impressive feature in many ways, but expect some false alarms and unwanted notifications. I strongly advise users to only turn on the specific sounds they absolutely need to be able to detect.
Note that the feature is off by default; you need to go into Settings on your iPhone, go to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition, turn on Sound Recognition, and finally turn on Detect using Apple Watch.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Music Recognition
This effectively changes Shazam from an actively triggered to a passive background function. The watch is continually listening out for music and will surface the information in the Smart Stack when it recognises it. (To turn this on, go into Settings on the watch, select Smart Stack, and then turn on Music Detection.)
Given my issues with Shazam being slow when manually triggered (see the previous section), and the risk of running out of song before it reaches a conclusion, this is handy. It isn’t quite instantaneous: when I bring up Smart Stack, it generally takes a couple of seconds for the Shazam widget to appear, or to refresh from the last song it recognised. But it’s much quicker and more reliable than when using that app manually, thanks to the information it harvests before you ask. Thumbs up.
Live Rewind
Now we get into the really interesting features… and also, sadly, the ones which aren’t available yet. The remaining Audio Intelligence features continue the theme of background listening, but add the faintly creepy twist that they’re monitoring your conversations.
Live Rewind is the simpler of the two. At any time (once it launches), you can double-press the Digital Crown, and it will display a transcript of the last 15 seconds. Very useful, presumably, if you struggle to remember all the specials and don’t want to ask the server to repeat themselves. Less effective if you’re trying to remember the start of a lengthy joke or anecdote.
Apple is aware of the privacy implications, and there are plenty of safeguards. The limited length of the transcription is one. Another is the effort to make sure people nearby are aware of what you’re doing: this is achieved via a trigger sound that can’t be silenced, an on-screen animation, and that hopefully recognisable double-press action. It also isn’t continuously recording. Only snippets that are called up and then expressly saved to the Siri app will be kept.
I really like the sound of this feature (particularly the relative lack of “AI-ness”), but I wish Apple would have delayed the announcement until it was actually ready.

				
					

				
			Didn’t quite catch that? Use Live Rewind. Eventually.
Apple




Siri Recap
This one’s a little more involved and a little more reliant on AI. Siri Recap listens in the background and makes notes on your conversations, which it will later summarise. The idea appears to be that you schedule or geofence the feature so it’s only listening when you’re at work, for example, or you can just turn it on and off manually. Or, I suppose, have it on all the time, but prepare for your friends and loved ones to be annoyed when they find out.
Bearing in mind the disastrous notification summaries we occasionally saw in the early days of Apple Intelligence, I will defer my thoughts on this until I can test its reliability.
New health sensors
Away from Audio Intelligence, the Series 12’s remaining headline new features return to the familiar worlds of health and fitness. Most notably, we have an entirely new “health sensing system” with a 2nd-gen electrical heart sensor.
Apple says the new sensor ensures better contact with the skin, and features redesigned photodiodes and larger, power-efficient green LEDs. It should therefore take more accurate readings. But it also takes, well, more readings. Whereas previous Apple Watch models measured the user’s heart rate on demand, during workouts, and every few minutes at other times, the Series 12 just does it constantly. Every five seconds, all day long, to what should be a high degree of accuracy.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




This may not seem like a big deal, because you may feel that any time you want to know your heart rate, you can ask for it. But firstly, this is a much more convenient way of accessing that information: there’s a new watch face complication for heart rate, so now you just need to glance down, and the number is right there. And more importantly, having access to heart-rate data all the time enables the Series 12 to reach more informed conclusions about the state of your health, your fitness, and even your stress levels.
The new sensor system also features a greater emphasis on HRV (or heart rate variability), a metric which doctors find useful in assessing heart health and physical recovery, and in diagnosing problems with sleep, stress, diet, and more. HRV was measured previously, but on the Series 12 is measured 24 times as often and is displayed in a new section of the Heart Rate app. But again, this is more likely to be useful in the way it feeds into broader insights surfaced in the Health app than in servicing the user’s sudden curiosity to know the number.
Readiness
The last new feature I want to talk about is the Readiness app. This is designed to distill a wide variety of health, sleep, HRV, and other metrics down into a single, easily comprehensible score out of 10 that indicates how ready your body is for an exercise session.
When I open the app now, for instance, it gives the verdict “9: Go For It.” When I scroll down, it expands on this to explain that my high sleep score from last night and my generally lower activity levels in recent days mean today is a great day to push hard.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




As ever, I like simplicity. The Apple Watch Series 12 has access to an enormous quantity of health data, but to the non-scientific layperson like myself, most of it is pretty close to incomprehensible. Boiling it down in this way makes it useful. There’s something I can do with that score.
And while this will doubtless vary from person to person, I can say that physical readiness for exercise is something I worry about a lot. As a fitness enthusiast in early middle age with an increasingly fragile body, I want to push the limits, but I don’t want to exceed them and end up with an injury or illness. Having the green light from Readiness will give me a great deal more confidence in the gym.
Note that Readiness needs a surprising amount of time to get ready: you need to wear it to bed for at least seven nights before it’s prepared to start delivering those verdicts. That’s fairly standard for such devices, and a Whoop or Fitbit will make similar demands for similar features. But I found it mildly frustrating that up to this point the app insisted on its main screen that there was “No Data,” even though scrolling down indicated that there was a great deal… just not yet enough. It might seem like a small quibble, but this seems a counterintuitive or even misleading way to handle setup.

				
					

				
			No data? What’s all that, then?
David Price / Foundry




The Readiness app, I’m happy to say, is available now. But wider integration of its findings will have to wait until the iOS 27.2 update, when the iPhone will get a redesigned version of the Health app. That will (among a lot of other new features) include a Readiness tab and the ability to look at Readiness data on your phone. iOS 27.2 should be here soon, and may even have arrived when you read this review; you can read more about the update here.
Apple Watch Series 12 battery
Officially the headline battery life hasn’t changed since last year: the estimate, as on the Series 11, remains “up to 24 hours.” (That, incidentally, was a big and surprising jump from the 18 hours which had been claimed for all ten previous Series models.) Our tests, however, indicate that this drastically underestimates what you can expect in typical daily usage. Whether longevity has improved or degraded from the previous generation is harder to say, since performance was wildly inconsistent.
The Series 11 was nice and steady. In each test, it lasted two days and two nights before expiring early on the morning of the third day: it managed 46 and 49 hours respectively for an average of 47.5 hours. In my review, I described that performance as superb, and I stand by that assessment.
The Series 12 did even better on its first run, making it to 10 am on the third day, for a total of 51 hours. I was rather blown away by this, especially bearing in mind the new inclusion of continual background heart-rate monitoring, which one might expect to have an impact on battery performance.
But then I ran a second test, and the Series 12 barely made it to bedtime on the second day, dying shortly after 11 pm: that’s a comparatively feeble 40 hours, and gives an average across the two runs of 45.5 hours. Leading to the conclusion that a) the Series 12 has slightly weaker battery performance than its predecessor on average and b) it’s also far, far less consistent in this department.
A degree of inconsistency is to be expected, because smartwatch battery tests are not an exact science; there’s no established benchmark we can use to directly compare devices. The precise time your Series 12 lasts will depend on what you do with it. (And it will obviously degrade over time.) The lit-up screen is obviously more of a power draw than the dimmed always-on version, and any active app usage will drain the battery quicker than having it run passively.
In the past, Workout has typically been one of the bigger battery sappers. It doesn’t seem especially worrisome these days: a 30-minute run on the treadmill with the companion iPhone nearby resulted in the Series 12 dropping from 99 percent to 97 percent, which isn’t too bad. But I will note that the second test, the one which fell so disastrously short of our expectations (while surpassing Apple’s, to be fair), included two longish walks with Workout in operation. That may have been a factor, although it could hardly be to blame for such a huge disparity.
While we’re on the topic, incidentally, Apple claims it has added some battery improvements specific to exercise sessions. Based on tests without an iPhone nearby, the company estimates that the Series 12 will last for 10 hours of outdoor workouts, which is a claimed 25 percent increase on the previous generation. If you plan to do a lot of ultramarathons, you may be better off with the new Apple Watch Ultra 4, which the company says is good for 18 hours of outdoor workouts, 25 hours with the new Extended Workout mode, and up to 45 hours with Max Extended Workout mode. (These modes are not available on the Series 12.)

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Fast-charging
Once the battery is drained, you’ll be able to top it up quickly… but maybe not quite as quickly as Apple thinks. The company says you can get from 0 to 80 percent with 30 minutes of fast-charging, but our tests suggest this is rather optimistic. Although, again, performance was frustratingly inconsistent.
Using the bundled charging puck and a big 67W power adapter, my Series 12 made it to just 58 percent in the assigned half hour, and took almost an hour to get to 80 percent. It was fully charged after 82 minutes. I repeated the test a few days later, and this time it went from 0 to 72 percent in half an hour (and was fully charged after 63 minutes). Those are wildly different results.
I compared notes with a colleague from Macwelt, who reported yet another result: their Series 12 managed 62 percent in half an hour. So with 30 minutes of charging (and a compatible and sufficiently powerful charger, of course) you can expect to boost your Series 12 from 0 to 58 percent, 62 percent, 72 percent, or some other number entirely. But don’t expect to make it to 80 percent, unless you’ve got access to the same mysterious super-chargers as Apple’s research team.
Those same Apple researchers claim that, if you’re pushed for time, 15 minutes of charging will get you enough power for 12 hours of normal use, which is an improvement on the 8 hours claimed for the Series 11. And in a real emergency, 5 minutes of charging just before bed should be enough for 10 hours of sleep tracking. My advice would be to take these claims with a pinch of salt.

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Apple Watch Series 12 price
The Series 12 starts at $399 if you plump for the smaller size and can manage without cellular. That’s the same price as the cheapest Series 11 model at launch last fall (the Series 11 is no longer available), which is a pleasant surprise: Apple raised the prices of its Macs, iPads, and iPhones this year in response to the global RAM shortage, so we were expecting something similar for the Apple Watch. Instead, it retains the same entry-level pricing.
It’s not all good news, as the larger 46mm versions of the Series 12 are a little more expensive than their equivalents in 2025. But these are mercifully small increases, compared with the carnage elsewhere.
Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm, GPS): From $399/£369
Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm, GPS + cellular): From $499/£469
Apple Watch Series 12 (46mm, GPS): From $449/£419
Apple Watch Series 12 (46mm, GPS + cellular): From $549/£519
Here’s the (surprisingly similar) pricing as of fall 2025:
Apple Watch Series 11 (42mm, GPS): From $399/£369
Apple Watch Series 11 (42mm, GPS + cellular): From $499/£469
Apple Watch Series 11 (46mm, GPS): From $429/£399
Apple Watch Series 11 (46mm, GPS + cellular): From $529/£499

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Should you buy the Apple Watch Series 12?
The Series 12 certainly isn’t a bad smartwatch. It looks great and feels comfortable on the wrist; the interface is easy to use; it has solid and at times exceptional battery life; and the latest upgrades mean it delivers the most accurate health and fitness data collection and analysis of any Apple product to date. I love the new Readiness app (a great concept, straightforwardly executed), and was very pleasantly surprised not to see a hefty price hike. There are many things to be cheerful about.
But compared to the achievements of the last generation, the excellent Series 11 and the outstanding SE 3 (what a shame we didn’t get an SE 4 this year, by the way), I can’t help feeling disappointed. The Series 12’s battery life and charging speed, while strong in isolation, are far less consistent than those of its predecessors, which means you can’t rely on a given level of performance when it really matters. There were uncharacteristic annoyances: a minor imperfection in the assembly, moments of sluggishness, repeated spontaneous resets. And most annoying of all, the product was launched with two of its flagship new features and full platform-wide integration of a third yet to launch to the public.
I feel like the teacher of a clever pupil who’s had a bad semester. Not bad. But I expected better.

title: Don't change the subject, Apple tells OpenAI over its lawsuit
content:

OpenAI is best known for creating ChatGPT but it is also working on hardware devices

title: John Ternus is already doing it all
content:
Macworld





John Ternus has now been CEO of Apple for over a month, so it’s time to rate his legacy. Okay, that’s probably unfair. Let’s give the guy at least a quarter.
But since we’re on the subject, what can we glean from what Ternus has done so far that will indicate what kind of CEO he’ll be? Admittedly, even that’s going to be hard because he’s barely had time to actually do anything, but there are some early indicators brought to us by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
Let’s start with somewhat vague concepts: Apple under Ternus: More products, more often, with a ‘leaner’ staff.
This reportedly includes being “more experimental” with releases. More experimental than the Vision Pro? Oookay. We’ll look forward to that.
Despite the desire to be leaner, Apple declined one… mmm, “opportunity” is the wrong word… “chance to punch itself in the face.” That’s more accurate: Apple Reportedly Planned to Replace 5,000 Support Employees With AI.
[Apple] worked on a plan to lay off about 5,000 AppleCare customer-service workers, including many who work from home, based on the belief that improved AI-powered phone and web agents could take over portions of their responsibilities. Apple ultimately put those plans on hold and isn’t currently looking to take such a step.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, September 29, 2026
Alas, Apple customers will not know the joys of having an AI ask us to do all the things we’ve already tried all over again before advising we log out of iCloud and then back in.
This might be another area where Apple supposedly being “late” to AI will work to its advantage as other companies have learned this lesson the hard way with three-quarters of them having rolled back AI call center deployments. In fact, instead of laying off the support personnel, Apple let go some middle managers and directors instead!

				
					

				
			
If you’d like to receive regular news and updates to your inbox, sign up for our newsletters, including The Macalope and Apple Breakfast, David Price’s weekly, bite-sized roundup of all the latest Apple news and rumors.

Foundry




Welcome to the class struggle, Apple Inc.? No, no, that’s not right. Ridiculous. Forget the Macalope said that.
Still, it’s worth noting that one Apple executive in particular is even having to do two jobs! And that executive is… oh! John Ternus! Apple’s John Ternus Has Found a New Design Chief: Himself.




15 years after Steve Jobs’ death, the design buck stops at the CEO’s desk once again. According to Gurman, gallant Ternus “works hands-on in the [Apple design] studio several times a week, sometimes visiting multiple times in a single day”, whereas Goofus Tim Cook would only visit “about an hour once a month, at most.” And he reportedly said things like “Is this one of them computers?” and “Does this one get the internet?”
Okay, maybe not that last part. Gurman drops a “many are saying” that really makes you wonder who his sources are.
Given design’s central role in Apple’s product development and in generating ideas for future devices, many people inside and close to the company believed it should recruit an outside chief design officer to oversee the entire organization. But I’m told no such search is underway.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, October 4, 2026
If many are, indeed, saying this, then those many should avail themselves of one of the various means by which one can get bent in today’s modern society. There are many options, please pick one of your choosing, because it is largely unfathomable as to who could just step into the role of chief freakin’ designer at Apple freakin’ Inc. Are Gurman’s sources people who think it should be them? Because this reads like one of those surveys of macho bros who think they could go a few rounds with a bear or a gorilla.
“Yeah, I think I could hold my own in a fight against a gorilla. I took a little taekwondo.”
Please, be the Macalope’s guest. Hope you don’t like using your arms because the gorilla is going to rip them off your body and beat you to death with them.
Anyway, this change just makes sense given the two CEOs’ different backgrounds and styles. It’s not like Cook’s tenure at Apple was anything other than a massive financial and operational success, but it’s still exciting to think this CEO is showing an interest in the details that make Apple products so compelling.
Are Ternus’s changes going to work? Heck if the Macalope knows. He would say we’ll have to wait until the rubber meets the road but Apple canceled the car project so that metaphor doesn’t work anymore. So far the horny one likes what he sees, though.

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours: Release date, OLED, specs and latest leaks
content:
Macworld





The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, the rumours are becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss.
Multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way. If they’re accurate, the first touchscreen MacBook Pro will arrive as part of one of the biggest redesigns in the laptop’s history, combining a new chassis with Apple’s first OLED MacBook display and potentially even an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout.
The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.
There are still questions over pricing. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures are expected to make the new models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro. Apple is also expected to keep touchscreen technology exclusive to its premium laptops initially, with no indication that it will come to the MacBook Air or MacBook Neo in the first generation. Read on for a complete roundup of the latest touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours, including what the most reliable sources are saying, how credible each report is, and what we think Apple is likely to announce and when.


Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
Late 2026 planned
Early 2027 a possibility
While Apple has yet to officially confirm the device, reports from respected analysts, supply-chain sources, and references discovered in Apple’s software all suggest development is well underway. The company is widely expected to launch a redesigned MacBook Pro featuring its first touchscreen OLED display, with the latest reporting pointing to an October or November 2026 launch, although Apple has not yet confirmed the product or its release date.
Speaking in a Power On podcast on October 1, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said he expected the touchscreen MacBook announcement as early as October, potentially slipping to November. The laptops are reportedly being tested with macOS 27.2.
In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction. In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8.6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.
However, the launch could still slip to early 2027. Global DRAM and NAND shortages, which prompted Apple to raise Mac and iPad prices in June 2026 – are expected to continue well into 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into until early 2027. He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule.In a July report, Gurman reiterated that these laptops are planned for this fall, but a 2027 ship date is possible.


						

							


Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen? 
Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips
Both Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo have reported that Apple is developing MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreen displays as part of a major redesign. The feature is expected to debut on the high-end MacBook Pro models powered by Apple’s Pro and Max chips, making them the first Macs to support direct touch input.
Apple is expected to use the touchscreen as a key differentiator for its professional laptops, further separating the MacBook Pro from the more affordable MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.
There is also speculation that Apple could rebrand the flagship model as the MacBook Ultra. According to one report from a source said to be familiar with Apple’s plans, the company intends to expand its “Ultra” branding beyond the Mac Studio and Apple silicon chips. However, this claim has not been corroborated by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman or analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, so it should be treated with caution.
For now, the technology appears set to remain exclusive to the MacBook Pro lineup. Neither the MacBook Air nor the MacBook Neo is expected to gain touchscreen support in the near term. However, Kuo believes Apple could eventually expand the technology to other MacBook models if the touchscreen MacBook Pro proves successful.
The MacBook Air may be the next candidate for a touchscreen upgrade, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely before 2028 or 2029. Some reports also indicate that the Air could adopt OLED display technology before then, albeit without touch functionality.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro Design
Thinner than the current MacBook Pro
Punch hole for the FaceTime camera
Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to have a thinner, substantially lighter design. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has focused on reworking the internal layout and reducing and consolidating components to improve portability. No specific weight or thickness has been confirmed.
One of the most significant visual changes could be the removal of the display notch. Reports from display analysts and Bloomberg suggest Apple may replace the current notch with a hole-punch camera cutout, allowing for more usable screen space around the sensor. In early 2026, Gurman went a step further, claiming the new MacBook Pro could adopt an iPhone-like Dynamic Island interface built around the camera cutout.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is also expected to retain its traditional laptop design, complete with a full keyboard and large trackpad, rather than becoming a hybrid tablet device.
Other rumoured design changes include:
A thinner and lighter chassis.
OLED display technology.
A hole-punch FaceTime camera replacing the notch.
Possible Dynamic Island-style functionality.
A reinforced hinge designed to minimise screen movement when the display is touched.
These changes would help distinguish the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the entry-level MacBook Neo while giving Apple’s flagship laptop its most substantial design update in years.


						

							


Which chip will feature in the touchscreen MacBook?
M5 Pro and M5 Max
Early rumours suggested the touchscreen MacBook Pro would debut with Apple’s M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. However, more recent reports indicate that Apple has revised its plans and will instead launch the first touchscreen MacBook with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors before moving directly to the M7 generation.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman in June 2026, Apple now plans to pair the redesigned MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than the previously rumoured M6 Pro and M6 Max. The report claims Apple may skip the M6 Pro/Max generation entirely to accelerate development of its AI-focused M7 chips, bringing them to market around six months earlier with significantly more powerful on-device AI capabilities.
While the ongoing DRAM and NAND shortages may also have influenced the decision, they are not thought to be the primary reason for the roadmap change. Apple has already raised Mac and iPad prices in response to higher memory costs.
The latest reports supersede earlier rumours that the touchscreen MacBook would feature M6-series processors built on TSMC’s 2nm process with a redesigned chip architecture. Leaked Apple files discovered by MacRumors in late 2025 also appeared to reference M6 MacBook Pro models, suggesting Apple was developing M6-based hardware before reportedly changing direction.
Separately, there has also been speculation that Apple could introduce its in-house 5G modem to a future MacBook Pro, enabling cellular connectivity without requiring Wi-Fi or an iPhone hotspot. However, this remains one of the least substantiated rumours surrounding the redesign.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Display
Tandem OLED display
Touchscreen interface
The display is expected to be the headline upgrade of Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro. Multiple reports suggest Apple will replace the current Liquid Retina XDR (mini-LED) panel with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing MacBook Pro technology closer to the Ultra Retina XDR display used in the latest iPad Pro.
According to analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, Apple is planning to introduce OLED touch panels in the MacBook Pro in late 2026 or early 2027. The new display is expected to be thinner, more power-efficient, and capable of delivering deeper blacks, higher contrast, richer colours, and improved HDR performance than today’s mini-LED screens.
Reports indicate that both the 14-inch and 16-inch models will use advanced tandem OLED technology, which combines two OLED layers to achieve higher brightness levels while maintaining excellent energy efficiency. Apple first introduced this technology with the M4 iPad Pro and is expected to bring a similar implementation to the MacBook Pro.
The touchscreen functionality will reportedly rely on on-cell touch technology, which integrates touch sensors directly into the display rather than adding a separate layer. This approach helps keep the panel thin while supporting multi-touch input.
If the rumours prove accurate, the move to a tandem OLED touchscreen would represent the biggest display upgrade in the MacBook Pro’s history and one of the most significant changes to the lineup in years.

				
					

				
			
The iPad Pro has a TaNdem OLED display, the type of display that could make its way into the 2026 MacBook Pro.

Brady Snyder / Foundry



							


Touchscreen MacBook Interface 

				
					

				
			
macOS 27 could have some hidden touchscreen features. 

Foundry




Apple is not expected to turn macOS into iPadOS, but reports suggest macOS 27 could include subtle design changes to make the Mac easier to use with touch input.
Rather than replacing the traditional desktop experience, Apple is reportedly working on a touch-tuned interface that adapts depending on how the device is being used. When touch input is detected, interface elements such as menus, buttons, and controls may automatically enlarge to make them easier to tap. When using a mouse or trackpad, macOS would revert to its familiar point-and-click layout.
The touchscreen itself is expected to support standard gestures such as tapping, scrolling, and zooming, while still allowing users to switch between touch, trackpad, and mouse input.
Further clues appeared in the macOS 27.2 beta on October 5. MacRumors reported new code references to touch gestures in Safari, Photos, Notes and Quick Look. These could support a future touchscreen MacBook, but they could also relate to Sidecar, which allows an iPad to act as a Mac display. 


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Connectivity 
5G connectivity could finally come to the Mac

				
					

				
			The C1X is now available,  but the C2 modem could be ready for the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Apple




Beyond the touchscreen display and redesigned chassis, one of the most intriguing rumours surrounding the next-generation MacBook Pro is built-in cellular connectivity.
Apple has spent the past several years developing its own modem technology, beginning with the C-series modem family. Reports suggest the company has explored bringing 5G connectivity to the MacBook lineup, allowing users to connect directly to mobile networks without relying on Wi-Fi or a smartphone hotspot.
Further evidence emerged in 2025 when Macworld contributor Filipe Esposito reported that Apple had tested an M5 MacBook Pro equipped with a 5G modem. While that feature did not make it into the final product, the report suggests Apple is actively evaluating cellular-enabled MacBooks.
The redesigned MacBook Pro could also benefit from Apple’s growing portfolio of wireless chips. The company’s N-series networking processors, which handle Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Thread connectivity, may eventually replace third-party components throughout the Mac lineup. An updated version of the chip could debut alongside the touchscreen MacBook Pro, improving power efficiency and tighter integration with Apple’s ecosystem.
While neither feature has been confirmed, Apple’s ongoing investment in modem and wireless technologies makes enhanced connectivity one of the more plausible additions to the redesigned MacBook Pro.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Price expectations
Apple will likely offer similar configurations to the current MacBook Pro models, but it’s unclear how much of a premium a touchscreen OLED display will command. Apple upped the price of the iPad Pro by $200 when it got a tandem OLED, so it’s likely the touchscreen MacBook Pro will have a higher starting price.
Here are the prices for the current standard configurations of the M5 MacBook Pro, which saw prices increase between $300 and $500 in June 2026.
14-inch MacBook Pro
$1,999/£1,999: M5 with a 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 4
$2,499/£2,499: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,099/£4,099: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
16-inch MacBook Pro
$2,999/£2,999: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,399/£4,399: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5

title: iOS 27.2 May Let You Hide Specific Suggested Actions in Messages
content:
iOS 27.2 is coming soon with several new features for iPhone users, including Suggested Actions in Messages, a feature that lets the Messages app offer actions based on the context of conversations.


If someone asks for a photo, Messages might suggest inserting it with a tap. If someone invites you to an event, Messages can suggest adding it to the Calendar app.

Suggested Actions in Messages originally appeared in the iOS 27 beta but was pulled in the final release. It's now back in the iOS 27.2 beta, and there's evidence that Apple is also adding finer manual controls over the one-tap action buttons so that users can turn them on and off individually. 

found the new controls in iOS 27.2 beta 3. A new settings screen provides separate toggles for Suggested Actions including Add to Calendar, Add to Reminders, Add to Notes, Show in Maps, and Flights and Packages.

There's also a switch to "Hide Unused Suggestions." When enabled, suggestions that aren't used will stop being shown in Messages after 30 days. Hidden suggestions can also be re-activated by toggling their individual switches off and back on again, according to the screenshot shared by pdfu.


Apple is working on granular controls for Suggested Actions in Messages, based on iOS 27.2 beta 3 code. https://t.co/Fbffdf7epy
— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 5, 2026



Apart from Suggested Actions in Messages, iOS 27.2 includes Apple's redesigned Health app with new Insight and Longevity tabs. It also brings Siri AI in new languages. There are several other new features, with details available in our features guide.

title: Latest macOS beta: What’s new and should you install it?
content:
Macworld





Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. Just two days later on September 16, Apple issued the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, beginning testing of the operating system’s next major point update. Yes, that’s macOS 27.2, not macOS 27.1. 
The macOS 27.2 beta gives developers and testers early access to Apple’s latest fixes, refinements and any features that weren’t ready for the initial Golden Gate release. 
However, as with any beta software, it may introduce bugs, compatibility problems and poorer battery life so we recommend caution if you wish to install it.
Here’s everything you need to know about the latest macOS beta, including what’s new, when the next public beta is likely to arrive and whether you should install it.


What’s the latest macOS beta? 
Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.
The latest Mac beta is macOS 27.2 beta 3, which Apple released to registered developers on October 5, 2026.
The corresponding macOS 27.2 public beta will be available soon. Public betas usually follow developer betas, although Apple does not guarantee a particular schedule.
macOS 27 Golden Gate beta version tracker 
Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Developer Beta 3 on October 5, 2026.
The macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Public Beta 2 arrived on September 22; new versions are usually released a day or two after the new developer beta.
macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.





macOS 27 Beta timeline


ReleaseDate
Beta 1June 8, 2026
Beta 2June 22, 2026
Beta 3July 6, 2026
Beta 3 v.2July 13, 2026
Beta 4July 20, 2026
Beta 5August 10, 2026
Beta 6August 17, 2026
Beta 7August 24, 2026
Beta 8August 31, 2026
Release Candidate 1September 9, 2026
Public Beta 1July 13, 2026
Public Beta 2July 22, 2026
Public Beta 3August 11, 2026
Public Beta 4August 17, 2026
Public Beta 5August 24, 2026
Public Beta 6August 31, 2026
Final ReleaseSeptember 14, 2026
macOS 27.2 developer beta 1September 16, 2026
macOS 27.2 developer beta 2September 21, 2026
macOS 27.2 developer beta 3October 5, 2026

 






What’s new in the latest beta?

				
					

				
			
New features in macOS 27.

Foundry




Apple has not announced any major consumer-facing additions in macOS 27.2 beta 2. The following changes are expected though:
Bug fixes and performance improvements: Addressing issues in the first release of macOS 27.
Additional Siri AI languages: Apple has said the Siri AI will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in October. 
Automatic password changes: The promised feature that automatically changes compromised passwords has not yet been implemented, but it could arrive in macOS 27.2.. 
We’ll update this section as changes are discovered.
See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta. 






Should you install the macOS beta?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.
Install if…
You need to test apps
You want early access to new features
You have a secondary Mac available
Wait if…
This is your primary work machine
You rely on niche or specialist software
Stability is critical to your workflow







Who are you Should you install?

A developer testing appsConsider the developer beta
An enthusiast with a spare MacConsider the public beta 
General user with one MacStay on macOS 27

 






What are the risks of installing beta software?
Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.
System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.






Safety precautions and best practices
If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:
Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.






How to install the macOS beta

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds. 
The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.
You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.
To install the beta follow these steps:
Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues. 
Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
Enable Beta Updates.
The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.
As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.
Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.






How to get a free Apple developer account
If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:
Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
Open the app on your iPhone. 
Tap on Account. 
Tap on Sign In. 
Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 
If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.






 FAQ 


1.
Who can run the macOS beta?
Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.
Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.
In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below. 
If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.





2.
macOS public beta vs developer beta
Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).
Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).
There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement
Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install. 
The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 
If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.





3.
Is the macOS beta stable?
By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 
If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:
We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.
We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.





4.
How to prepare your Mac for the beta
Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.
Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!
Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.





5.
How to send feedback to Apple
Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.
You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.
It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.
If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.





6.
Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?
Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.  





7.
Can I talk about the beta publicly?
According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”
However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.





8.
How to downgrade from the macOS beta
You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.
Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.





9.
Is the beta free to download? 
Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.





10.
Can I go back to the stable version?
Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.
If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.





11.
Should I install the beta on my main Mac?
Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.





12.
Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?
You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.





13.
How often are new beta versions released?
New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.





14.
Is the macOS beta safe to install?
The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.





15.
Will my apps work with the macOS beta?
Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

title: Apple and AT&T Have Yet to Explain Cause of iPhone 18 Pro Max Issue
content:
In a statement shared with MacRumors on Friday, Apple said that iPhone 18 Pro Max users who have experienced an issue where AT&T cellular service does not work will need to have the device replaced, as the issue apparently cannot be fixed with a software update once it has occurred. This requirement is a big deal, as it hints at hardware failure, but we lack details since Apple and AT&T have yet to disclose the underlying cause of the issue.


A spokesperson for AT&T directed us to Apple, which has yet to respond to our latest request for comment. It is possible that Apple is still investigating the issue, but so far our follow-up questions have been met with radio silence (pun intended).

iOS 27.0.1 and an AT&T carrier settings update released last week "are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring," so iPhone 18 Pro Max users who have not experienced this issue should ensure that both of these updates are installed immediately to avoid potential future impacts.

To install iOS 27.0.1, open the Settings app on your iPhone and tap General → Software Update. 

The carrier settings update for the iPhone 18 Pro Max will automatically download for AT&T users within the next 14 days, according to Apple. To manually trigger the update, users can open the Settings app and tap General → About.

Apple said it has only observed this issue with iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network. No other iPhone models or carriers are known to be impacted.

title: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max recall explained: Is Qualcomm to blame?
content:
Macworld





The launch of the iPhone 18 Pro Max has been anything but smooth for AT&T users. Ever since the phone started shipping two weeks ago, reports have been cropping up about an inability to make calls, send texts, or even call emergency services. Considering we’re talking about a phone, it’s a serious issue.
In a statement to Macworld and other media outlets, Apple said that “a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network” with phones that have already been affected by the issue will need to get them replaced. If you bought an AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max, here’s what you need to know.
Update: Added a section explaining whether the problem will definitely be fixed with a replacement phone.
What is the problem?
Apple has identified an issue that specifically stops the iPhone 18 Pro Max from accessing AT&T’s network, preventing users from making calls and sending texts. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro, which was released at the same time, does not exhibit the same issue, nor do iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on Verizon or T-Mobile.
The issue doesn’t appear to affect all AT&T phones, however. While there have been numerous reports from AT&T subscribers with iPhones that haven’t been able to make calls ever since they got the phone, others only experienced the issue after a few days, and still others haven’t had it at all. It’s not clear what triggers the issue.
Can Apple fix it?
Last week, Apple pushed out iOS 27.0.1 to fix a Face ID bug and other launch-day issues with the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The AT&T bug wasn’t listed in the release notes, but AT&T urged its subscribers to install the update as a potential fix. The carrier also pushed out its own update to iPhone 18 Pro Max users that will roll out over the next two weeks.
However, we have since learned that those fixes only prevent the problem from occurring in future; they don’t fix phones that are already exhibiting the issue. In fact, Apple and AT&T both acknowledge that phones with the problem will need to be replaced with a phone that already has iOS 27.0.1 and AT&T’s carrier settings update installed.
Is there an official recall?
Apple has only issued two iPhone recalls in its history, and both offered repairs rather than replacements. In 2021, Apple began a program to fix iPhone 12 or iPhone 12 Pro units that did not emit sound from the receiver when making or receiving calls, and in 2024, iPhone 14 Plus owners who could not see previews when taking photos with the rear camera were also eligible for free repairs.
So, while this is the first time Apple is specifically offering replacement devices, Apple hasn’t declared an official service program. However, if your phone experiences the issue, you should contact AT&T or Apple to swap it out for a new phone.
Will a new phone definitely fix the issue?
It seems as though the problem has been mitigated with a new iPhone 18 Pro Max running iOS 27.0.1 and AT&T’s carrier update. However, Macworld was contacted by a technician familiar with the issue who has dealt with some 50 cases. However, they report that some customers who received replacements still reported frequent outages and issues with cellular connectivity. However, these phones did not have both the iOS update and AT&T’s settings fix applied.
Since AT&T’s fix is rolling out over the coming weeks, it’s possible that a replacement phone will exhibit the same issues. So unless it’s a matter of urgency, it might be better to wait a few days until we have more clarity, or an official statement from Apple.
Why isn’t the iPhone 18 Pro affected?
Neither Apple nor AT&T have divulged the specific issue with the iPhone 18 Pro Max that affects its ability to access data. There’s very little about the phone that isn’t identical to the iPhone 18 Pro other than the size of the screen and battery, but there is one notable component that’s different: the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a Qualcomm modem rather than an Apple one.
According to teardowns, it’s the same modem as the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, the Snapdragon X80 5G Modem, and neither of those phones exhibit the issue. And even though Apple is offering replacement phones, the issue appears to be a software one related to how the hardware interacts specifically with AT&T’s network.
It’s not clear why the iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple’s most expensive phone that doesn’t fold, uses an older Qualcomm modem in the U.S. rather than Apple’s new C2 modem, which supports mmWave networks for the first time. (In other countries, the 18 Pro Max does have a C2.) Indeed, a lot of older and cheaper iPhones have C-class Apple modems too: last year’s iPhone Air has the C1X, as does the iPhone 17e. The iPhone 16e from February 2025 featured a C1… but the more expensive iPhone 16 has a Qualcomm modem. It’s all quite complicated.
I have an AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max. What should I do?
This depends on whether you’ve experienced the symptoms described above. 
If your iPhone appears to have escaped the bug so far, install iOS 27.0.1 right now. (Open Settings, go to General > Software Update, and follow the prompts.) You’ll also want the latest carrier settings update. This should download automatically within the next 14 days, but you can manually trigger the process by opening Settings and going to General > About.
If you have experienced the problems… well, it’s still worth installing the updates because this is free and takes almost no time. There’s always the extremely slim possibility that you were suffering from an unrelated bug and it may be fixed by a patch or go away by itself. But realistically, you’re going to need a replacement phone. Assuming the problems persist, contact Apple Support or AT&T, or visit an Apple Store or AT&T location.
But your mileage may vary. A reader with one of the affected phones reached out and said he was sent to the Apple Store after trying Best Buy (where he bought the phone) and an AT&T store after neither had any information about the recall. Eventually he found an Apple representative who tested the phone and agreed to ship a replacement device. We expect Apple will announce an official program to address the issue soon.

Which MacBook should you buy?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Apple’s current MacBook range falls into three clear categories:
MacBook Air M5: Best MacBook for most people
The M5 MacBook Air is our default recommendation for most buyers. It combines strong performance, long battery life and portability without the higher price of a MacBook Pro. With no replacement expected until 2027, a good Prime Day discount would be easy to recommend.
MacBook Neo: Best budget MacBook
The MacBook Neo is the cheapest MacBook and is best suited to students and anyone who mainly needs a laptop for web browsing, documents, streaming and video calls. If a discounted MacBook Air is only moderately more expensive, however, the Air is the better long-term buy.
MacBook Pro M5: Best for demanding work
The MacBook Pro is the better choice for video editing, software development, 3D work and other demanding tasks that benefit from sustained performance. Prime Day discounts could be worthwhile, although a redesigned MacBook Pro is rumored before the end of 2026.
MacBook Pro M5 Pro/Max: Best for professional workloads
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max model if you need significantly more CPU and GPU performance, additional memory or greater connectivity. If you already own an M4 Pro or M4 Max model, there is little reason to upgrade.
For most Prime Day shoppers, we recommend starting with the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo becomes especially compelling when heavily discounted, while MacBook Pro buyers should consider whether they need the additional performance and professional features enough to justify the considerably higher price.
